blocks.content: The story starts at the worst possible moment.

A user clicks "Pay Now" on your checkout page. The request leaves their browser, crosses the internet, hits your payment service, your payment service calls Stripe, Stripe charges their card and then the network dies. Not before the charge. After. The response never makes it back. The browser times out. The user sees a spinner, then an error page.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027811-937703811.png
blocks.alt: A payment request with no visible response leads directly to the question of whether clicking pay again charges twice

blocks.content: They click "Pay Now" again. Did you just charge them twice?

This is the idempotency problem. Not a theoretical edge case this happens millions of times per day across every distributed system on the planet. Networks are unreliable. Servers crash. Clients retry. The question is never "will retries happen?" It's "what happens when they do?"
1. Definition and Why It Matters

Idempotency is the property that makes retries safe. An operation is idempotent if performing it multiple times has exactly the same effect as performing it once. The first request charges the card. The second request the retry recognises it's a duplicate and returns the same result without charging again.
In mathematics, idempotent means applying the same operation multiple times produces the same result as applying it once.
In distributed systems, idempotency means a request can be retried any number of times, but the final result remains exactly the same as if it were executed only once.

This is important because in distributed systems, a client often doesn't know what happened to its request. The request may have been lost, processed successfully but the response was lost, partially processed before a crash, or completed successfully while the client timed out. From the client's perspective, all these situations look the same it simply receives no response or a timeout.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275732847-110576074.png
blocks.alt: Not every HTTP method behaves the same way when a client retries it

blocks.content: Since the client cannot know what actually happened, the safest action is to retry the request. Without idempotency, each retry could execute the operation again, causing problems like duplicate payments, duplicate orders, or duplicate emails.
With idempotency, the server detects that the request has already been processed, usually using an Idempotency Key, and simply returns the original response instead of executing the operation again.
2. HTTP methods and Natural idempotency
HTTP methods have defined idempotency semantics. Understanding these is foundational.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275734402-535792678.png
blocks.alt: PUT and DELETE are naturally idempotent, PATCH depends on the operation, and POST needs an explicit idempotency key

blocks.content: Not all HTTP methods are idempotent. Some can be safely retried, while others may produce different results each time.

["PUT is idempotent because it replaces a resource with the same data every time. For example, sending PUT /users/123 with name = \"Alice\" multiple times always leaves the user named Alice.
","DELETE is also idempotent. The first request deletes the resource, and any later requests simply find that the resource is already gone. The final state remains the same.
","PATCH depends on the operation. If it sets a value, such as balance = 100, it is idempotent because repeating the request produces the same result. However, if it increments a value, such as balance += 10, it is not idempotent because every retry changes the balance again.
","POST is not idempotent by default. Every retry can create a new resource or trigger the same action again, leading to duplicate orders, payments, or emails. This is why POST requests usually use Idempotency Keys to make retries safe.
"]
items: PUT is idempotent because it replaces a resource with the same data every time. For example, sending PUT /users/123 with name = "Alice" multiple times always leaves the user named Alice.
DELETE is also idempotent. The first request deletes the resource, and any later requests simply find that the resource is already gone. The final state remains the same.

PATCH depends on the operation. If it sets a value, such as balance = 100, it is idempotent because repeating the request produces the same result. However, if it increments a value, such as balance += 10, it is not idempotent because every retry changes the balance again.

POST is not idempotent by default. Every retry can create a new resource or trigger the same action again, leading to duplicate orders, payments, or emails. This is why POST requests usually use Idempotency Keys to make retries safe.

blocks.content: Key Takeaway: PUT and DELETE are naturally idempotent, PATCH depends on the operation, and POST requires an Idempotency Key to safely handle retries.
3. Idempotency keys: making POST safe

An Idempotency Key is a unique identifier generated by the client and sent with a request. The server uses this key to determine whether the same request has already been processed. If the key already exists, the server returns the previous response instead of executing the operation again.
First Request
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027811-305993281.png
blocks.alt: A brand new idempotency key gets processed normally and its response stored for later

blocks.content: When the client sends a POST request with a new idempotency key, the server first checks its idempotency store.
Since the key is not found, it processes the request normally, stores the response against that key, and returns the result to the client.
Retry Request
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028311-388688715.png
blocks.alt: A retry with the same idempotency key returns the stored response instead of running the operation again

blocks.content: If the client does not receive the response because of a timeout or network failure, it retries the same request using the same idempotency key. This time, the server finds the key in its idempotency store and immediately returns the cached response.
The operation is not executed again, so duplicate payments or duplicate resource creation are avoided.
Result: From the client's perspective, both requests receive the same response. Internally, however, the operation was executed only once. The retry becomes completely transparent and safe.
Why Does the Client Generate the Key?
blocks.text: Why Does the Client Generate the Key?

blocks.content: The idempotency key should always be generated by the client, not the server. If the server generated the key, the client would first need to request a key before sending the actual request. This adds an extra network call and still doesn't solve the retry problem if the key-generation request itself fails.
Characteristics of a Good Idempotency Key
blocks.text: Characteristics of a Good Idempotency Key

blocks.content: A good idempotency key should be unique for every operation, not for every user or session. A UUID is commonly used.
The same key must be reused for every retry of the same logical operation. Changing the key on every retry makes the server treat it as a completely new request.

The key should also represent the same request. A common practice is to generate it using a unique value (such as a UUID) or derive it from the request data so that identical retries always use the same key.
4. Implementing the idempotency store

An Idempotency Store keeps track of every processed request using the Idempotency Key. Whenever a request arrives, the server first checks this store. If the request has already been processed, it simply returns the previously stored response instead of executing the operation again.
A typical idempotency record contains:

Schema:
  key:        string  (client-provided UUID)
  status:     integer (HTTP status code to return)
  response:   blob    (serialised response body)
  created_at: timestamp
  expires_at: timestamp (TTL — typically 24h to 30d)
  in_flight:  boolean (true while first request is processing)

blocks.content: Redis is the most common choice because it provides fast lookups, built-in TTL support, and atomic operations.
1. The Concurrent Request Problem
The biggest challenge is when two identical requests arrive at exactly the same time.
Without Protection: Both requests check Redis. Neither finds the key. Both start processing. Both complete successfully.
Result: The operation is executed twice (for example, the customer is charged twice).
2. With an Atomic Lock
Before processing the request, the server creates an "in-flight" marker using Redis SET NX.
Only the first request succeeds. The second request immediately knows another request is already processing the same operation and returns 409 Conflict(or waits and retries).
This guarantees that only one request performs the business operation.
3. Implementation
The implementation follows a simple flow:check the idempotency key, acquire an atomic lock, execute the business logic, store the response, and return the cached result for all future retries.
Step 1: Check whether the request already exists
blocks.text: Step 1: Check whether the request already exists

blocks.content: Whenever a request arrives, first check Redis.
If the request has already completed, return the cached response. If another request is still processing it, return 409 Conflict.
Step 2: Acquire an Atomic Lock
Now try to create an in-flight marker. Redis SET NX guarantees that only one request succeeds.
The 5-minute TTL is important.
If the server crashes while processing, the lock automatically expires so future retries can continue.
Step 3: Execute the Business Logic
Only the request that acquired the lock executes the actual operation.
PaymentResponse response = paymentService.processPayment(request);
This is where the payment is charged, the order is created, or the email is sent.
Step 4: Store the Final Response
Replace the temporary lock with the actual response.

Step 5: Return the Response
return response;
blocks.text:
Step 5: Return the Response
return response;

blocks.content: The client receives the response normally.
Step 6: Cache Error Responses Too
Failures should also be stored.
If the first request returns an error, every retry receives the same error instead of executing the operation again.
Complete Flow & Code
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028312-940439188.png
blocks.alt: Every request checks the idempotency store first, processing only if the key has never been seen before

blocks.content:
["Why Use Redis?: Redis provides O(1) lookups, built-in TTL, and atomic commands like SET NX. This makes it ideal for storing idempotency records and preventing duplicate processing.
","Why Use SET NX?: SET NX means Set Only If Not Exists. It is an atomic operation, so even if two identical requests arrive at exactly the same moment, only one request acquires the lock. The other request immediately knows the operation is already in progress, preventing duplicate payments or duplicate resource creation.
","Why Is TTL Important?: The lock must expire automatically. If the server crashes after acquiring the lock but before finishing the request, the TTL removes the stale lock after a few minutes. Without a TTL, the request could remain locked forever and every future retry would fail.
"]
items: Why Use Redis?: Redis provides O(1) lookups, built-in TTL, and atomic commands like SET NX. This makes it ideal for storing idempotency records and preventing duplicate processing.

Why Use SET NX?: SET NX means Set Only If Not Exists. It is an atomic operation, so even if two identical requests arrive at exactly the same moment, only one request acquires the lock. The other request immediately knows the operation is already in progress, preventing duplicate payments or duplicate resource creation.

Why Is TTL Important?: The lock must expire automatically. If the server crashes after acquiring the lock but before finishing the request, the TTL removes the stale lock after a few minutes. Without a TTL, the request could remain locked forever and every future retry would fail.

blocks.content: 5. Idempotency in databases
Idempotency isn't only at the HTTP layer. The same principle applies at the database level.
1. Natural database idempotency
Databases can prevent duplicate operations using unique constraints. This acts as the final safety net if duplicate requests reach the database.

-- Not idempotent: every retry creates a new row
INSERT INTO orders (user_id, product_id, amount)
VALUES (123, 456, 99.99);

-- Idempotent: duplicate requests are ignored
INSERT INTO orders (user_id, product_id, amount, idempotency_key)
VALUES (123, 456, 99.99, 'uuid-A')
ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING;

-- Idempotent: sets the same value every time
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = 100
WHERE id = 123;

-- Not idempotent: every retry increments the value
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 10
WHERE id = 123;

Similarly, setting a value (balance = 100) is idempotent, while incrementing a value (balance = balance + 10) is not.
2. The Outbox Pattern and Idempotency
The Outbox Pattern ensures that both the database update and event creation happen atomically.

BEGIN TRANSACTION;

-- Save business data

INSERT INTO orders
(id, user_id, amount, idempotency_key)
VALUES
(gen_uuid(), 123, 99.99, 'uuid-A')
ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING;

-- Save the event in the same transaction

INSERT INTO outbox
(event_type, payload, idempotency_key)
VALUES
('OrderCreated', '{"order_id":"..."}', 'uuid-A')
ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING;

COMMIT;

If the transaction succeeds, both records are saved. If it fails, neither is saved. Later, a CDC tool (such as Debezium) reads the Outbox table and publishes the event to Kafka. If the event is published more than once, consumers use theidempotency_keyto detect and ignore duplicates.
6. Idempotency in message queues and event systems
blocks.text: 6. Idempotency in message queues and event systems

blocks.content: Message queues like Kafka usually guarantee at-least-once delivery, which means the same event can be delivered multiple times. Because of this, consumers must be idempotent so that processing the same event again does not create duplicate records or perform the same action twice.

["Natural idempotency: The simplest approach is to design operations that are naturally safe to repeat. For example, updating a record to a specific value is safer than incrementing it, and using UPSERT is safer than creating a new row every time. Even if the same event is processed multiple times, the final result remains the same.
","Deduplication store: Another common approach is to maintain a store of processed event IDs in Redis or a database. Before processing an event, the consumer checks whether the event ID already exists. If it has already been processed, the event is skipped. Otherwise, it is processed and its ID is stored. This prevents duplicate processing even if Kafka delivers the same event multiple times.
","Transactional processing: For systems that require the strongest consistency, the business operation and the message acknowledgement are committed together in a single transaction. This ensures that either both succeed or both fail, providing exactly-once processing semantics. Although this offers the highest level of reliability, it is also the most complex approach.
"]
items: Natural idempotency: The simplest approach is to design operations that are naturally safe to repeat. For example, updating a record to a specific value is safer than incrementing it, and using UPSERT is safer than creating a new row every time. Even if the same event is processed multiple times, the final result remains the same.

Deduplication store: Another common approach is to maintain a store of processed event IDs in Redis or a database. Before processing an event, the consumer checks whether the event ID already exists. If it has already been processed, the event is skipped. Otherwise, it is processed and its ID is stored. This prevents duplicate processing even if Kafka delivers the same event multiple times.

Transactional processing: For systems that require the strongest consistency, the business operation and the message acknowledgement are committed together in a single transaction. This ensures that either both succeed or both fail, providing exactly-once processing semantics. Although this offers the highest level of reliability, it is also the most complex approach.

blocks.content: 7. The key design decisions

A good idempotency implementation is not just about generating an idempotency key. You also need to decide how long to store it, what happens while a request is still being processed, and how to handle retries with different request data.
1. TTL (Time To Live)
Idempotency records should not be stored forever. Each record has a Time To Live (TTL), after which it is automatically removed.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028049-213424211.png
blocks.alt: An idempotency record needs a TTL long enough to cover the realistic retry window without expiring too early

blocks.content:
["If the TTL is too short, the record may expire before the client finishes retrying. A later retry will be treated as a brand-new request and processed again, resulting in duplicate operations.
","If the TTL is too long, the system wastes storage by keeping records that will never be used again.
"]
items: If the TTL is too short, the record may expire before the client finishes retrying. A later retry will be treated as a brand-new request and processed again, resulting in duplicate operations.
If the TTL is too long, the system wastes storage by keeping records that will never be used again.

blocks.content: The TTL should always be longer than the maximum retry window of your clients.
Typical values used in production are:
["Payment APIs: 24 hours","Financial transactions: 30–90 days","Emails and notifications: 24 hours","Resource creation: 24 hours to 7 days"]
items: Payment APIs: 24 hours
Financial transactions: 30–90 days
Emails and notifications: 24 hours
Resource creation: 24 hours to 7 days

blocks.content: For example, if clients retry requests for up to one hour, storing the idempotency record for 24 hours provides a safe buffer.
2. Request found but still in progress
blocks.text: 2. Request found but still in progress

blocks.content: Sometimes the client retries before the original request has finished processing.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396028313-14348724.png
blocks.alt: A retry that arrives mid-processing never restarts the operation, it gets a 409, a delayed cached response, or a status URL instead

blocks.content: In this situation, the server should never start processing the request again. Instead, it can respond in one of three ways.
The simplest approach is to return 409 Conflict, informing the client that the request is already being processed and should be retried later.
Another approach is to wait for a few seconds. If the original request completes during that time, the server immediately returns the cached response. Otherwise, it returns 409 Conflict.

For long-running operations, such as video processing or report generation, a common approach is to return 202 Accepted along with a status URL. The client can periodically check this URL until the operation completes.
For most APIs, returning 409 Conflict is the simplest and most common solution.
3. Retry with a different request body
blocks.text: 3. Retry with a different request body

blocks.content: An idempotency key should always represent one logical operation.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785275744137-534850733.png
blocks.alt: Reusing the same idempotency key with a different request body is rejected, since one key must represent one logical operation

blocks.content: Suppose the first request is:
Idempotency-Key: uuid-AAmount: 100
Later, another request arrives with the same key:
Idempotency-Key: uuid-AAmount: 200
Although the idempotency key is the same, the request itself is different.

The server should compare the new request with the original request stored against that key. If the request body is different, it should return 422 Unprocessable Entity instead of processing the request.
This prevents accidental key reuse, client bugs, or key collisions from producing incorrect results.

A good practice is to store a hash of the original request body along with the idempotency key and compare it on every retry. If the hashes match, return the cached response. If they differ, reject the request. This guarantees that a single idempotency key can never be used for two different operations.
8. Where idempotency appears in real systems
blocks.text: 8. Where idempotency appears in real systems

blocks.content:
["Stripe: the Idempotency-Key header is a core feature of their API, documented on every write endpoint. Every retry of a payment, every retry of a refund, uses the same key. Stripe stores the result for 24 hours. Their implementation is the gold standard.
","AWS: S3 PUT is naturally idempotent (same object key = replace in place). SQS supports deduplication IDs for exactly-once processing within a 5-minute window. DynamoDB's conditional writes (ConditionExpression) enable idempotent updates.
","Kafka producer: enable.idempotence=true makes the producer idempotent: even if a message is retried, it's written to the topic exactly once. Sequence numbers and producer IDs enable deduplication.
","Database migrations: tools like Flyway and Liquibase are idempotent. Running a migration twice doesn't corrupt the schema because each migration is tracked by ID.
"]
items: Stripe: the Idempotency-Key header is a core feature of their API, documented on every write endpoint. Every retry of a payment, every retry of a refund, uses the same key. Stripe stores the result for 24 hours. Their implementation is the gold standard.

AWS: S3 PUT is naturally idempotent (same object key = replace in place). SQS supports deduplication IDs for exactly-once processing within a 5-minute window. DynamoDB's conditional writes (ConditionExpression) enable idempotent updates.
Kafka producer: enable.idempotence=true makes the producer idempotent: even if a message is retried, it's written to the topic exactly once. Sequence numbers and producer IDs enable deduplication.
Database migrations: tools like Flyway and Liquibase are idempotent. Running a migration twice doesn't corrupt the schema because each migration is tracked by ID.

blocks.content:
REST DELETE: a well-designed API returns 200 or 204 on the first successful delete and also 200 or 204 (not 404) on subsequent deletes. The effect of the operation (resource is gone) is the same regardless of how many times you call it. 

Some APIs return 404 on the second delete this technically satisfies the idempotency definition (the resource is still gone) but breaks client retry logic that treats 404 as a failure.

blocks.content: 9. HLD Interview ( How to Talk About Idempotency )
blocks.text: 9. HLD Interview ( How to Talk About Idempotency )

blocks.content: ["Explain the problem: Clients retry requests when they don't receive a response. Without idempotency, retries can create duplicate payments, orders, or emails.","Explain the solution: The client sends a unique Idempotency Key with every request. The server checks whether the key already exists. If it does, it returns the cached response; otherwise, it processes the request and stores the result.","Handle concurrent requests: If two requests with the same key arrive together, use Redis SET NX so only one request is processed. The others receive 409 Conflict.","Handle server failures: Store the in-flight key with a TTL. items: Explain the problem: Clients retry requests when they don't receive a response. Without idempotency, retries can create duplicate payments, orders, or emails.

Explain the solution: The client sends a unique Idempotency Key with every request. The server checks whether the key already exists. If it does, it returns the cached response; otherwise, it processes the request and stores the result.
Handle concurrent requests: If two requests with the same key arrive together, use Redis SET NX so only one request is processed. The others receive 409 Conflict.
Handle server failures: Store the in-flight key with a TTL. If the server crashes, the lock expires automatically and future retries can continue safely.
Protect the database: Add a unique constraint on the idempotency_key (for example, ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING) to prevent duplicate records even if duplicate requests reach the database.
Where to use it: Idempotency is essential for payments, order creation, inventory reservation, email sending, and other write operations where duplicate execution is unacceptable.
